title: Shallow Water Equations
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The shallow water equations model a thin layer of fluid under gravity by coupling depth-averaged momentum to mass conservation, forming a hyperbolic system with wave speed sqrt(gh).
short: Long gravity waves travel at speed sqrt(g times depth).
long: Long gravity waves travel at speed sqrt(g times depth). They admit shocks interpreted as hydraulic jumps and bore waves.
proof: Integrate the incompressible Euler equations over the thin layer and assume hydrostatic pressure and small vertical acceleration.
consequence: They model tides, tsunamis, and river flooding.

title: Korteweg–de Vries Soliton
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The Korteweg–de Vries equation admits solitary travelling waves whose speed is proportional to their amplitude and which survive collisions almost unchanged.
short: Dispersion balances nonlinearity to create a stable pulse.
long: Dispersion balances nonlinearity to create a stable pulse. The equation is integrable and possesses an infinite hierarchy of conserved quantities.
proof: Insert the travelling-wave ansatz, integrate twice using decay at infinity, and verify the sech-squared profile.
consequence: It founded soliton theory with applications to water waves and fibre optics.

title: Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation and Bright Solitons
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The focusing cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation supports bright solitons whose dispersion is exactly balanced by self-focusing nonlinearity.
short: Self-focusing traps the wave against spreading.
long: Self-focusing traps the wave against spreading. The defocusing sign instead supports dark solitons on a nonzero background.
proof: Insert the ansatz into the equation and match real and imaginary parts, using the sech differential equation.
consequence: It models optical fibres, Bose–Einstein condensates, and deep-water envelopes.

title: Burgers' Equation and Shock Formation
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: The viscous Burgers equation combines nonlinear steepening with diffusion; in the inviscid limit it develops shock waves selected by the entropy condition.
short: Nonlinearity sharpens waves while viscosity smooths them.
long: Nonlinearity sharpens waves while viscosity smooths them. The Cole–Hopf transform linearises the viscous equation to the heat equation.
proof: Set u = -2 nu (phi_x/phi) to reduce Burgers to the heat equation for phi, then study the zero-viscosity limit.
consequence: It is the simplest model for shock formation and turbulence analogies.

title: Rankine–Hugoniot Conditions
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Across a shock discontinuity, conservation laws require the jump in flux to equal the shock speed times the jump in the conserved quantity.
short: Conservation dictates how fast a discontinuity can move.
long: Conservation dictates how fast a discontinuity can move. An additional entropy condition selects the admissible branch of solutions.
proof: Integrate the conservation law over a shrinking space-time pillbox around the shock and let its width tend to zero.
consequence: It determines shock speeds in gas dynamics and traffic flow.

title: Helmholtz Equation and the Sommerfeld Radiation Condition
subject: Applied Mathematics
statement: Time-harmonic wave scattering is governed by the Helmholtz equation, and outgoing solutions are selected by requiring decay of the radial derivative in the far field.
short: The radiation condition forbids waves arriving from infinity.
long: The radiation condition forbids waves arriving from infinity. It ensures uniqueness for exterior boundary value problems at real wave numbers.
proof: Expand the solution in outgoing Hankel functions and show the condition excludes the incoming branch.
consequence: It is essential for well-posed acoustic and electromagnetic scattering problems.

title: The Discrete Logarithm Problem in Number Theory
subject: Number Theory
statement: Given a prime p, a generator g of the multiplicative group modulo p and an element h, the discrete logarithm problem asks for an integer x with g^x congruent to h modulo p.
short: Finding exponents modulo a prime is believed to be hard even though exponentiation is easy.
long: Finding exponents modulo a prime is believed to be hard even though exponentiation is easy. The problem is defined in any finite cyclic group, including elliptic curve groups.
proof: Exponentiation is efficiently computable by repeated squaring, while known classical algorithms for inversion, such as baby-step giant-step, require roughly sqrt of the group order operations.
consequence: Its presumed hardness underlies Diffie–Hellman key exchange and ElGamal encryption.

title: Noether's First Theorem on Continuous Symmetries
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Every continuous symmetry of the action of a physical system yields a conserved quantity.
short: Symmetry and conservation laws are two sides of one coin.
long: Symmetry and conservation laws are two sides of one coin. Time-translation symmetry gives energy, spatial translation gives momentum, and rotation gives angular momentum.
proof: Invariance of the Lagrangian up to a total derivative implies, via the Euler–Lagrange equations, that a specific combination of momenta and the gauge term is constant along solutions.
consequence: It is the organising principle of modern field theory and explains conservation laws from geometry.

title: The Euler–Lagrange Equations of Variational Calculus
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: A curve that extremises an action integral of the form integral of L(q,q',t) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations on its interior.
short: Extremising an integral gives a differential equation for the extremal curve.
long: Extremising an integral gives a differential equation for the extremal curve. The brachistochrone and minimal surface problems are classical applications.
proof: Consider a variation q+epsilon η vanishing at endpoints, differentiate the action with respect to epsilon at zero, integrate the eta-prime term by parts and use the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations.
consequence: It converts variational principles into the equations of motion of classical mechanics.

title: Hamilton's Canonical Equations of Motion
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: In canonical coordinates (q,p), the dynamics of a Hamiltonian system is governed by q-dot equals the partial derivative of H with respect to p and p-dot equals minus the partial derivative with respect to q.
latex: \dot q=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p},\quad \dot p=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}
short: Hamiltonian mechanics trades second-order equations for a symmetric first-order system.
long: Hamiltonian mechanics trades second-order equations for a symmetric first-order system. Hamilton's equations preserve the symplectic form on phase space.
proof: Apply the Legendre transform to the Lagrangian and vary the phase-space action; integration by parts gives the two canonical equations.
consequence: It is the bridge from classical to quantum mechanics and to symplectic geometry.

title: The Poisson Bracket as a Lie Algebra Structure
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Poisson bracket of functions f and g on phase space is sum over i of (partial f/partial q_i partial g/partial p_i minus partial f/partial p_i partial g/partial q_i), and it satisfies the Jacobi identity.
latex: \{f,g\}=\sum_i\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q_i}\right)
short: Observables form a Lie algebra under the Poisson bracket.
long: Observables form a Lie algebra under the Poisson bracket. The time derivative of any observable is its Poisson bracket with the Hamiltonian plus an explicit time derivative.
proof: The bracket is bilinear, antisymmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity by direct differentiation; the evolution formula follows from the chain rule and Hamilton's equations.
consequence: It is the classical counterpart of the quantum commutator.

title: The Legendre Transform and Convex Duality
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Legendre transform of a convex function f is f*(p)=sup over x of (px−f(x)), and for differentiable strictly convex f it is an involution.
short: The Legendre transform swaps a function with the family of its tangent-line intercepts.
long: The Legendre transform swaps a function with the family of its tangent-line intercepts. It converts a Lagrangian into a Hamiltonian and appears throughout convex optimisation.
proof: If f is convex and differentiable, the supremum occurs where p=f'(x); applying the transform again recovers f by the supporting-line characterisation of convexity.
consequence: It is the mathematical engine behind Hamiltonian mechanics and convex duality.

title: The Principle of Stationary Action
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Physical trajectories make the action functional stationary under small variations with fixed endpoints, rather than necessarily minimal.
short: Nature picks paths where first-order changes of the action vanish.
long: Nature picks paths where first-order changes of the action vanish. Stationary includes minima, maxima and saddle points; Fermat's principle of least time is a related variational principle.
proof: For a one-parameter family of paths with fixed endpoints, the first derivative of the action vanishes exactly when the Euler–Lagrange equations hold.
consequence: It unifies mechanics, optics and field theory in a single variational language.

title: The Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The state of a nonrelativistic quantum system evolves according to iħ times the time derivative of the wavefunction equals the Hamiltonian operator acting on it.
short: Quantum time evolution is generated by the Hamiltonian through a first-order equation.
long: Quantum time evolution is generated by the Hamiltonian through a first-order equation. For a time-independent Hamiltonian the solution is exp(−iHt/ħ) applied to the initial state.
proof: The equation is a postulate of quantum mechanics; when H is time-independent, exponentiation of the self-adjoint operator gives a unitary evolution group by Stone's theorem.
consequence: It predicts interference, tunnelling and the entire spectroscopy of atoms and molecules.

title: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For position and momentum observables, the product of their standard deviations in any state is at least ħ/2.
short: Position and momentum cannot both be sharply localised.
long: Position and momentum cannot both be sharply localised. The inequality is a consequence of the noncommutation of the corresponding operators and is not a measurement imperfection.
proof:
Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to (X−)ψ and (P−

)ψ and use the commutator [X,P]=iħ.
consequence: It sets fundamental limits on precision and explains the zero-point energy of quantum systems.

title: Canonical Quantisation and the Commutation Relations
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Canonical quantisation replaces classical phase-space variables by operators satisfying [q_i,p_j]=iħ δ_ij and replaces Poisson brackets by commutators divided by iħ.
short: Quantum mechanics is obtained by turning classical brackets into operator commutators.
long: Quantum mechanics is obtained by turning classical brackets into operator commutators. The correspondence is a guiding rule rather than a rigorous functor and has ordering ambiguities for nonlinear expressions.
proof: Dirac's rule identifies the classical Poisson bracket structure with the commutator algebra of observables; the Stone–von Neumann theorem gives uniqueness of the representation for finitely many degrees of freedom.
consequence: It provides the standard route from classical to quantum theories.

title: The Pauli Matrices and Spin-One-half
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The three Pauli matrices are Hermitian 2 by 2 matrices whose pairwise products give i times the remaining matrix; they represent spin-one-half observables and satisfy σ_i σ_j = δ_ij I + i ε_ijk σ_k.
short: A pair of complex matrices encodes the algebra of spin.
long: A pair of complex matrices encodes the algebra of spin. They also generate the fundamental representation of SU(2) and square to the identity.
proof: Direct multiplication of the explicit matrices gives the anticommutation and commutation relations.
consequence: They are the building blocks of two-level quantum systems and of the Dirac equation.

title: The Dirac Equation for Relativistic Spinors
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Dirac equation (i γ^μ ∂_μ − m)ψ=0 is a relativistic wave equation whose gamma matrices satisfy the Clifford algebra relations and whose solutions describe spin-one-half particles and antiparticles.
short: Factoring the relativistic energy relation yields a first-order equation with spin built in.
long: Factoring the relativistic energy relation yields a first-order equation with spin built in. The gamma matrices satisfy {γ^μ,γ^ν}=2η^{μν}I, and squaring the operator recovers the Klein–Gordon equation.
proof: Dirac found matrices whose anticommutators reproduce the Minkowski metric, so applying the conjugate operator gives the relativistic dispersion relation.
consequence: It predicted antimatter and is the foundation of relativistic quantum field theory.

title: Lorentz Transformations and the Invariance of the Speed of Light
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Transformations between inertial frames preserve the spacetime interval c²t²−x²−y²−z² and form the Lorentz group.
short: Different observers disagree about space and time but agree on the spacetime interval.
long: Different observers disagree about space and time but agree on the spacetime interval. They lead to time dilation and length contraction and contain rotations as a subgroup.
proof: Requiring the speed of light to be the same in all inertial frames and the transformations to be linear forces preservation of the Minkowski quadratic form.
consequence: It is the geometric foundation of special relativity.

title: The Stress–Energy Tensor and Local Conservation Laws
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The stress–energy tensor encodes the density and flux of energy and momentum, and its divergence vanishes in the absence of external forces.
short: Local conservation of energy and momentum is expressed by a vanishing divergence.
long: Local conservation of energy and momentum is expressed by a vanishing divergence. In general relativity the partial derivative becomes a covariant derivative, and the tensor acts as the source of gravity.
proof: Noether's theorem applied to spacetime translations yields four conserved currents, assembled into T^{μν}; their divergence vanishes on the equations of motion.
consequence: It is the universal language for energy transport in field theories.

title: Maxwell's Equations in Differential Form
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Using exterior calculus, Maxwell's equations become dF=0 and d star F = J, where F is the electromagnetic field two-form and J the current three-form.
short: The four Maxwell equations compress into two geometric statements.
long: The four Maxwell equations compress into two geometric statements. The first equation implies the existence locally of a potential one-form A with F=dA.
proof: Writing the electric and magnetic fields as components of F and applying the exterior derivative reproduces the homogeneous Maxwell equations; the codifferential gives the inhomogeneous ones.
consequence: This formulation makes gauge invariance and relativistic covariance transparent.

title: Gauge Invariance and Covariant Derivatives
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Replacing ordinary derivatives by covariant derivatives built from a connection makes field equations invariant under local symmetry transformations.
short: Gauge fields compensate for spacetime-dependent symmetry rotations.
long: Gauge fields compensate for spacetime-dependent symmetry rotations. The curvature of the connection is the gauge field strength.
proof: Under a local gauge transformation the connection changes inhomogeneously so that D_μψ transforms covariantly; the commutator of covariant derivatives gives the curvature, which transforms homogeneously.
consequence: It is the common structure underlying electromagnetism, Yang–Mills theory and general relativity.

title: The Aharonov–Bohm Effect
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Charged particles can be affected by an electromagnetic potential in a region where the electric and magnetic fields vanish, through the topology of the configuration space.
short: Even with zero field, a nontrivial potential can shift quantum phases.
long: Even with zero field, a nontrivial potential can shift quantum phases. It demonstrates that gauge potentials have physical significance beyond the classical fields.
proof: Electrons travelling around a solenoid enclosing magnetic flux acquire a relative phase equal to the enclosed flux in appropriate units, producing a measurable interference shift.
consequence: It reveals the role of topology and holonomy in quantum physics.

title: Yang–Mills Gauge Theory and Field Strength
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Yang–Mills theory generalises electromagnetism to nonabelian gauge groups, with field strength given by the curvature F=dA+A∧A and equations D star F=0.
short: Noncommuting gauge symmetries produce self-interacting force fields.
long: Noncommuting gauge symmetries produce self-interacting force fields. The nonabelian term A∧A is what makes the theory nonlinear.
proof: The field strength arises as the commutator of covariant derivatives, and the Yang–Mills equations are the Euler–Lagrange equations of the action integral of tr(F∧star F).
consequence: It describes the strong and weak nuclear interactions.

title: The Gauge Group of the Standard Model
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Standard Model of particle physics is based on the gauge group SU(3) times SU(2) times U(1), describing the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions.
short: Three symmetry groups organise all known elementary particles and forces except gravity.
long: Three symmetry groups organise all known elementary particles and forces except gravity. Spontaneous symmetry breaking reduces the electroweak part to electromagnetic U(1).
proof: Matter fields are assigned representations of the group; requiring local gauge invariance forces the introduction of gauge bosons transforming under the adjoint representation.
consequence: It is the most thoroughly tested framework in fundamental physics.
